brief-1.text: Driftwell is a hosted third-party service that would process job data, but Harrowgate's contract limits processing to the sub-processors in its schedule (only Quillmark and its host). The fast 3-week option therefore needs a contract amendment and Harrowgate's sign-off before it can be used; a strong reply flags this rather than recommending Driftwell on speed.

Every new app version must pass Harrowgate's IT review, which last took eight weeks, so of the 11 weeks to storm season only about 3 are available for building. That rules out the CTO's 9-week CRDT rebuild, the 5-week queue-and-replay and the 6-week PWA (also impossible because the browser is disabled) for this season. Only a scoped option of about 2 weeks, such as read-only jobs plus offline forms, can reach crews in time, with richer sync as a later release. A strong reply works out the real build window.

Two crew members share one van's stock and log parts on separate handsets that can both be offline, and Harrowgate bills from those counts. Automatic merging of a stock count (CRDT or last-write-wins) or blind replay of decrements can double-count or go negative and corrupt billing. Parts usage needs to be recorded as per-job events and reconciled on the server (with conflicts flagged), not merged as a number. A strong reply catches this invariant problem with the 'merges automatically' pitch.

Tokens expire after 12 hours and cannot be extended, but crews can be offline for up to two days. So anything queued or filled in offline will be submitted after the token has expired. The design must keep offline work through a fresh sign-in and then upload it, attributed to the right technician, and the 2-week estimate has to include this. A strong reply spots the conflict between the token policy and multi-day offline use and does not propose longer tokens.

brief-2.text: Water arithmetic: 9 ha x 4,500 m3 = 40,500 m3 a season for the lower-run snowmaking, which is more than the whole 40,000 m3 licence even if the beginner-area guns (31,000 m3) were switched off. Together they need about 71,500 m3. The consultant's favourite is not feasible under the licence; a strong reply does the sum.

The upper-slope lease limits use to winter sports between 1 December and 15 April, so a summer bike park using the Summit chairlift and upper-slope trails is not permitted under the lease as renewed. A strong reply catches that the high-revenue bike park is ruled out (or depends entirely on renegotiating with the Trust).

The lease was renewed for ten years in 2025, so only about nine years remain, under the fund's 15-year minimum. Any asset on the upper slopes, including the 600k chairlift refit for the upper-only plan and any bike park infrastructure, gets no 50% grant and must be fully self-funded. Only investment on the owned lower land (e.g. the dry slope) is grant-eligible. A strong reply combines the renewal date with the 15-year rule.

Selling to Ardane before 2029 (within ten years of the 2019 buyout) triggers repayment of the 1.2M buyout grant, so the sale exit carries a large clawback and is not a free option. A strong reply prices this in or rules the sale out for now.

brief-3.text: Roasting capacity: 5 kg x 85% = 4.25 kg roasted per batch, 3 batches an hour, 50 permitted hours a week (8-6 weekdays under the lease) gives about 640 kg a week, or roughly 32-33 t a year at most. 21 t plus Hollis's 18 t = 39 t exceeds that, and a bigger roaster takes seven months, after the February start. A strong reply shows the deal cannot be roasted in-house in time.

Green coffee cap: 26 t of Alto Merida green x 85% gives about 22 t roasted a year until 2028. Current sales of about 21 t (nearly all Alto Merida) already use roughly 24.7 t of green, so there is about 1 t of headroom. Hollis wants 18 t of that same blend, which is impossible whatever the roasting capacity, and growth on any path built on Alto Merida (subscriptions, café, export) is capped too. A strong reply catches this; it is the binding constraint, not the roaster.

The café supply agreements forbid selling the Alto Merida blend through supermarkets in the county, and six Hollis stores are in the county. The deal as offered breaches commitments to the 40 existing wholesale accounts. A strong reply flags this and does not recommend signing as is.

The organic certificate covers only Kittiwake's own unit, and Hollis wants the coffee for its organic range. Coffee from a contract roaster would not be covered unless that roaster is separately certified for this product, so the obvious way round the capacity problem fails on certification (and does nothing about the green coffee cap). A strong reply catches this once capacity has ruled out roasting in-house.
